title: The throne room (Revelation 4)
hook: a rainbow, a sea of glass, creatures crying holy

segments.voice: Yesterday, Laodicea: lukewarm, and yet someone standing at the door, knocking. Your line was I stand at the door. Who knocked, and did you open? Day one thousand two hundred ninety-seven.

Yesterday's letter ended with a door, and Christ outside it, knocking. Today the door swings the other way. "After this I looked, and, behold, a door was opened in heaven." A voice like a trumpet says, "Come up hither." The letters to the seven churches are done. John, the exile on Patmos, is invited up through the door, and finds himself looking into the room that the rest of the book keeps coming back to. The throne room. Today we stand in the doorway with him and look.
screen: `THE ROOM THE BOOK KEEPS COMING BACK TO.`

segments.voice: First, the throne, and the one who sits on it. John doesn't describe a face. Only light and stone: "he that sat was to look upon like a jasper and a sardine stone: and there was a rainbow round about the throne, in sight like unto an emerald." Some readers hear, in that rainbow, the bow God set in the clouds after the flood, a sign of promise. John doesn't say. He just reports the green light circling the throne. Second, around it: twenty-four elders in white with crowns of gold, lightning and thunder, and "before the throne there was a sea of glass like unto crystal." Clear as crystal. The text doesn't explain the sea; it lets you stand at the edge of it. Third, the creatures. The King James calls them beasts; the sense is living creatures. One is like a lion, one like a calf, one has the face of a man, one is like a flying eagle. They're full of eyes, they have six wings, and "they rest not day and night, saying, Holy, holy, holy, Lord God Almighty, which was, and is, and is to come." It echoes the prophet Isaiah, who heard seraphim cry, "Holy, holy, holy, is the LORD of hosts." A later Christian tradition matched the four faces to the four Gospel writers, and you may still see a lion, an ox and an eagle carved on a pulpit. Fourth, what the elders do. Every time the creatures sing, the elders fall down and "cast their crowns before the throne." Whatever honor they were given, they lay it down. In some churches' communion services, the congregation joins that same song: holy, holy, holy.

Here's the practice: picture the throne room. Settle, and close your eyes if that's comfortable. Breathe. Let a rainbow appear, green as an emerald, curved around a light you don't try to look into. At your feet, a sea of glass, perfectly still. Somewhere, a sound that never stops, soft and steady, like breathing. If you pray, you can join the creatures' words, slowly, one on each breath: holy, holy, holy. If you don't, just stay at the edge of the glass and let the stillness hold you. The bell holds the time.
The throne room. John's vision through an open door in heaven: a rainbow like emerald, a sea of glass, and creatures who never stop saying holy.
Your line: holy, holy, holy. Today, when a sky, a face or a piece of music catches you, stay with it a moment longer and let it be holy. Day one thousand two hundred ninety-seven.

howItsDone: In the communion services of some churches, the congregation sings or says the 'Holy, holy, holy' (the Sanctus), joining the song of Isaiah 6 and Revelation 4, and the hymn 'Holy, Holy, Holy! Lord God Almighty' draws on this chapter.
